Existing defenses, such as prompt engineering and safety fine-tuning, often introduce computational overhead, increase inference latency, and lack runtime flexibility. Moreover, overly restrictive safety measures can degrade model utility by causing refusals of benign queries. In this paper, we introduce Jailbreak Antidote, a method that enables real-time adjustment of LLM safety preferences by manipulating a sparse subset of the model's internal states during inference. By shifting the model's hidden representations along a safety direction with varying strengths, we achieve flexible control over the safety-utility balance without additional token overhead or inference delays. Our analysis reveals that safety-related information in LLMs is sparsely distributed; adjusting approximately 5% of the internal state is as effective as modifying the entire state. Extensive experiments on nine LLMs (ranging from 2 billion to 72 billion parameters), evaluated against ten jailbreak attack methods and compared with six defense strategies, validate the effectiveness and efficiency of our approach. By directly manipulating internal states during reasoning, Jailbreak Antidote offers a lightweight, scalable solution that enhances LLM safety while preserving utility, opening new possibilities for real-time safety mechanisms in widely-deployed AI systems.

papers.title: Towards Understanding Safety Alignment: A Mechanistic Perspective from Safety Neurons
papers.research_question: How does safety alignment work in large language models from a mechanistic perspective, and can we identify specific neurons (safety neurons) responsible for safety behaviors?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies sparse safety neurons in LLMs that are causally responsible for safety behaviors, and shows that patching these neurons can restore safety performance. It also explains alignment tax by showing that safety and helpfulness share overlapping neurons but require different activation patterns.
papers.conclusion: The work provides a mechanistic understanding of safety alignment through safety neurons, demonstrating their causal role, transferability, and application in safeguards, paving the way for more robust alignment algorithms.
papers.key_findings:
Safety neurons are sparse (about 5% of neurons) and causally effective, with patching restoring over 90% of safety performance.
Safety neurons encode transferable mechanisms, effective across multiple red-teaming benchmarks without sacrificing general ability.
Safety neurons are robust to training randomness, with high overlap across different training runs.
Alignment tax arises because safety and helpfulness alignment share overlapping neurons but require different activation patterns for the same neurons.
Safety neurons can be used to build an effective safeguard that detects unsafe outputs before generation, improving model safety.
papers.limitation:
Safety neurons require activations from already aligned models; training-free methods to obtain these activations are not explored.
The alignment used (IA)3, a parameter-efficient method, while real-world models often undergo full fine-tuning; the impact of this difference is unknown.
The paper identifies which neurons affect safety but not how they exert this influence.
future_direction: Exploring training-free methods to obtain safety neuron activations.
Investigating how safety neurons exert their influence (the specific mechanisms).
Studying the evolution of safety neurons during pre-training.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) excel in various capabilities but pose safety risks such as generating harmful content and misinformation, even after safety alignment. In this paper, we explore the inner mechanisms of safety alignment through the lens of mechanistic interpretability, focusing on identifying and analyzing safety neurons within LLMs that are responsible for safety behaviors. We propose inference-time activation contrasting to locate these neurons and dynamic activation patching to evaluate their causal effects on model safety. Experiments on multiple prevalent LLMs demonstrate that we can consistently identify about $5\%$ safety neurons, and by only patching their activations we can restore over $90\%$ of the safety performance across various red-teaming benchmarks without influencing general ability. The finding of safety neurons also helps explain the ''alignment tax'' phenomenon by revealing that the key neurons for model safety and helpfulness significantly overlap, yet they require different activation patterns for the same neurons. Furthermore, we demonstrate an application of our findings in safeguarding LLMs by detecting unsafe outputs before generation. The source code is available at https://github.com/THU-KEG/SafetyNeuron.

papers.title: Towards Understanding and Improving Refusal in Compressed Models via Mechanistic Interpretability
papers.research_question: How does the refusal mechanism change in compressed models, and why are quantized models safer than pruned ones? Additionally, how can we improve the safety of compressed models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that compressed models retain a single-direction refusal mechanism, but pruning alters this direction leading to safety loss, and introduces AIRD to improve safety of compressed models without performance degradation.
papers.conclusion: The refusal mechanism changes in pruned models, explaining safety loss, and AIRD can effectively improve safety without harming performance.
papers.key_findings:
The refusal mechanism is still mediated by a single direction in compressed models.
In pruned models, the source position of the refusal direction changes, while in quantized models it remains the same.
The change in refusal direction correlates with loss of safety in pruned models.
Quantized models are safer than pruned models because they retain the original refusal direction.
AIRD can improve safety of pruned models without significant performance loss.
papers.limitation:
Findings may not generalize to non-transformer architectures like Mixture of Experts, State Space Models, and RNNs.
AIRD reduces the compression rate by decreasing sparsity in one layer.
future_direction: Generalize findings to non-transformer architectures.
Optimize AIRD to mitigate compression rate reduction.
papers.abstract: The rapid growth of large language models has spurred significant interest in model compression as a means to enhance their accessibility and practicality. While extensive research has explored model compression through the lens of safety, findings suggest that safety-aligned models often lose elements of trustworthiness post-compression. Simultaneously, the field of mechanistic interpretability has gained traction, with notable discoveries, such as the identification of a single direction in the residual stream mediating refusal behaviors across diverse model architectures. In this work, we investigate the safety of compressed models by examining the mechanisms of refusal, adopting a novel interpretability-driven perspective to evaluate model safety. Furthermore, leveraging insights from our interpretability analysis, we propose a lightweight, computationally efficient method to enhance the safety of compressed models without compromising their performance or utility.

papers.title: Tell Me What You Don't Know: Enhancing Refusal Capabilities of Role-Playing Agents via Representation Space Analysis and Editing
papers.research_question: How do existing models perform when facing different types of conflicting queries? Why is there a gap in RPAs' abilities to handle different types of conflicting queries? How can we enhance RPAs' ability to respond to conflicting queries without compromising their general role-playing capabilities?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a representation editing method that shifts conflicting queries in the representation space to enhance refusal capabilities of role-playing agents without training, and provides analysis of representation spaces to explain refusal behavior.
papers.conclusion: The representation editing approach offers a promising solution for enhancing RPAs' refusal capabilities without training, maintaining role-playing abilities.
papers.key_findings:
Models show significant performance gaps between contextual and parametric knowledge conflict queries.
Analysis reveals rejection and direct response regions in the model's representation space, which influence refusal behavior.
The proposed representation editing method effectively improves refusal accuracy without compromising general role-playing capabilities.
papers.limitation:
The method is tested on models with 7-8B parameters and may not scale to larger models (70B+).
The applicability of representation editing to other domains beyond role-playing is not explored.
future_direction: Extending the representation editing approach to larger state-of-the-art models (70B+).
Exploring the applicability of representation editing in other domains.
papers.abstract: Role-Playing Agents (RPAs) have shown remarkable performance in various applications, yet they often struggle to recognize and appropriately respond to hard queries that conflict with their role-play knowledge. To investigate RPAs' performance when faced with different types of conflicting requests, we develop an evaluation benchmark that includes contextual knowledge conflicting requests, parametric knowledge conflicting requests, and non-conflicting requests to assess RPAs' ability to identify conflicts and refuse to answer appropriately without over-refusing. Through extensive evaluation, we find that most RPAs behave significant performance gaps toward different conflict requests. To elucidate the reasons, we conduct an in-depth representation-level analysis of RPAs under various conflict scenarios. Our findings reveal the existence of rejection regions and direct response regions within the model's forwarding representation, and thus influence the RPA's final response behavior. Therefore, we introduce a lightweight representation editing approach that conveniently shifts conflicting requests to the rejection region, thereby enhancing the model's refusal accuracy. The experimental results validate the effectiveness of our editing method, improving RPAs' refusal ability of conflicting requests while maintaining their general role-playing capabilities.

papers.title: Mitigating Safety Tax via Distribution-Grounded Refinement in Large Reasoning Models
papers.research_question: How does distributional gap in safety alignment datasets cause reasoning degradation (safety tax) in large reasoning models, and how can it be mitigated?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes DGR, a data refinement method that aligns safety datasets with the target model's distribution to mitigate safety tax, and shows that distribution shift correlates with reasoning degradation and that safety alignment acts as a knowledge activation mechanism.
papers.conclusion: Distribution shift induced by safety alignment is a primary driver of reasoning degradation in LRMs; DGR mitigates safety tax by aligning safety data with the model's native distribution, and safety alignment functions as a latent-knowledge activator.
papers.key_findings:
DGR effectively mitigates safety tax, improving average reasoning accuracy by +30.2% on DirectRefusal and +21.2% on R1-ACT compared to Vanilla SFT.
The degree of reasoning degradation correlates with the extent of distribution shift, suggesting bridging this gap is central to preserving reasoning capability.
Safety alignment in LRMs may primarily function as a mechanism to activate latent knowledge, as a mere 10 samples are sufficient for activating effective refusal behaviors.
DGR is robust to refinement templates and generalizes to larger model scales (tested on 32B).
Fixed safety templates lead to over-refusal and low lexical diversity, highlighting the need for nuanced safety.
papers.limitation:
Not extending DGR to RL-based safety alignment pipelines.
Limited scaling to massive reasoning models (only tested up to 32B due to computational constraints).
future_direction: Extending DGR to reinforcement learning–based safety alignment pipelines.
More comprehensive evaluations on LRMs with larger parameter scales (e.g., 70B and beyond).
papers.abstract: Safety alignment incurs safety tax that perturbs a large reasoning model's (LRM) general reasoning ability. Existing datasets used for safety alignment for an LRM are usually constructed by distilling safety reasoning traces and answers from an external LRM or human labeler. However, such reasoning traces and answers exhibit a distributional gap with the target LRM that needs alignment, and we conjecture such distributional gap is the culprit leading to significant degradation of reasoning ability of the target LRM. Driven by this hypothesis, we propose a safety alignment dataset construction method, dubbed DGR. DGR transforms and refines an existing out-of-distributional safety reasoning dataset to be aligned with the target's LLM inner distribution. Experimental results demonstrate that i) DGR effectively mitigates the safety tax while maintaining safety performance across all baselines, i.e., achieving \textbf{+30.2\%} on DirectRefusal and \textbf{+21.2\%} on R1-ACT improvement in average reasoning accuracy compared to Vanilla SFT; ii) the degree of reasoning degradation correlates with the extent of distribution shift, suggesting that bridging this gap is central to preserving capabilities. Furthermore, we find that safety alignment in LRMs may primarily function as a mechanism to activate latent knowledge, as a mere \textbf{10} samples are sufficient for activating effective refusal behaviors. These findings not only emphasize the importance of distributional consistency but also provide insights into the activation mechanism of safety in reasoning models.

papers.title: GSAE: Graph-Regularized Sparse Autoencoders for Robust LLM Safety Steering
papers.research_question: How to effectively steer LLMs for safety by capturing distributed safety representations using graph-regularized sparse autoencoders?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Graph-Regularized Sparse Autoencoders (GSAE) to capture distributed safety representations in LLMs, enabling effective runtime safety steering with high refusal rates and preserved utility.
papers.conclusion: GSAE provides a robust method for safety steering by learning distributed safety representations, achieving high safety discrimination and utility preservation across diverse models and attacks.
papers.key_findings:
GSAE steering achieves an average 82% selective refusal rate, substantially outperforming standard SAE steering (42%).
It maintains strong task accuracy on QA benchmarks (e.g., 70% on TriviaQA, 65% on TruthfulQA, 74% on GSM8K).
GSAE generalizes across multiple LLM families (LLaMA-3, Mistral, Qwen, Phi) and scales.
It is robust against jailbreak attacks (GCG, AutoDAN), consistently maintaining ≥90% refusal of harmful content.
Ablation studies show that graph regularization is essential for performance, and the dual-gating mechanism enables adaptive steering.
papers.limitation: The runtime steering mechanism incurs inference latency overhead, which can interfere with optimized serving engines.
future_direction: Decomposing distributed features into interpretable safety sub-categories.
Ensuring the robustness of the neuron co-activation graph to dataset biases and adversarial inputs.
Extending graph-regularized learning to multi-modal domains.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) face critical safety challenges, as they can be manipulated to generate harmful content through adversarial prompts and jailbreak attacks. Many defenses are typically either black-box guardrails that filter outputs, or internals-based methods that steer hidden activations by operationalizing safety as a single latent feature or dimension. While effective for simple concepts, this assumption is limiting, as recent evidence shows that abstract concepts such as refusal and temporality are distributed across multiple features rather than isolated in one. To address this limitation, we introduce Graph-Regularized Sparse Autoencoders (GSAEs), which extends SAEs with a Laplacian smoothness penalty on the neuron co-activation graph. Unlike standard SAEs that assign each concept to a single latent feature, GSAEs recover smooth, distributed safety representations as coherent patterns spanning multiple features. We empirically demonstrate that GSAE enables effective runtime safety steering, assembling features into a weighted set of safety-relevant directions and controlling them with a two-stage gating mechanism that activates interventions only when harmful prompts or continuations are detected during generation. This approach enforces refusals adaptively while preserving utility on benign queries. Across safety and QA benchmarks, GSAE steering achieves an average 82% selective refusal rate, substantially outperforming standard SAE steering (42%), while maintaining strong task accuracy (70% on TriviaQA, 65% on TruthfulQA, 74% on GSM8K). Robustness experiments further show generalization across LLaMA-3, Mistral, Qwen, and Phi families and resilience against jailbreak attacks (GCG, AutoDAN), consistently maintaining >= 90% refusal of harmful content.

papers.title: Attributional Safety Failures in Large Language Models under Code-Mixed Perturbations
papers.research_question: Why do safety guardrails in large language models fail under code-mixed perturbations, and how can this be explained and mitigated?
papers.core_contribution: The paper uncovers attributional collapse as a cause of safety failures in LLMs under code-mixed inputs, introduces the Saliency Drift Attribution (SDA) framework to explain it, and proposes a lightweight translation-based restoration strategy.
papers.conclusion: Code-mixing poses a serious and overlooked safety risk for LLMs, driven by attributional collapse, but interpretability methods like SDA can guide practical mitigation strategies.
papers.key_findings:
Attack Success Rates (ASR) spike from ~9% in monolingual English to ~69% under code-mixed inputs, with rates exceeding 90% in languages like Arabic and Hindi.
The Saliency Drift Attribution (SDA) framework shows safety-critical tokens lose attributional salience under code-mixing, blinding the model to harmful intent.
A translation-based restoration strategy recovers roughly 80% of the safety lost to code-mixing.
Safety failures persist on real-world social media data (TRAC-1), confirming the vulnerability is not an artifact of synthetic data.
The degree of safety degradation increases monotonically with the intensity of code-mixing (e.g., higher embedded language ratio).
papers.abstract: While LLMs appear robustly safety-aligned in English, we uncover a catastrophic, overlooked weakness: attributional collapse under code-mixed perturbations. Our systematic evaluation of open models shows that the linguistic camouflage of code-mixing -- ``blending languages within a single conversation'' -- can cause safety guardrails to fail dramatically. Attack success rates (ASR) spike from a benign 9\% in monolingual English to 69\% under code-mixed inputs, with rates exceeding 90\% in non-Western contexts such as Arabic and Hindi. These effects hold not only on controlled synthetic datasets but also on real-world social media traces, revealing a serious risk for billions of users. To explain why this happens, we introduce saliency drift attribution (SDA), an interpretability framework that shows how, under code-mixing, the model's internal attention drifts away from safety-critical tokens (e.g., ``violence'' or ``corruption''), effectively blinding it to harmful intent. Finally, we propose a lightweight translation-based restoration strategy that recovers roughly 80\% of the safety lost to code-mixing, offering a practical path toward more equitable and robust LLM safety.

papers.title: Spot Risks Before Speaking! Unraveling Safety Attention Heads in Large Vision-Language Models
papers.research_question: How can internal activations of large vision-language models, specifically attention heads, be used to detect malicious prompts and understand inner safety mechanisms?
papers.core_contribution: Discovers safety attention heads in LVLMs that can detect malicious prompts and constructs an efficient, tuning-free defender (SAHs) based on these heads.
papers.conclusion: Leveraging safety attention heads effectively protects LVLMs from malicious prompts with minimal inference overhead, as confirmed by experiments across various attacks.
papers.key_findings:
Activations from attention heads can linearly separate malicious prompts from benign ones.
Sparse attention heads generate strongly discriminative features for identifying malicious inputs.
Safety heads act as specialized shields; ablating them reduces model safety without affecting utility.
The reduced number of safety heads in LVLMs increases their vulnerability compared to LLMs.
The constructed detector using safety heads shows strong zero-shot generalization capabilities.
papers.abstract: With the integration of an additional modality, large vision-language models (LVLMs) exhibit greater vulnerability to safety risks (e.g., jailbreaking) compared to their language-only predecessors. Although recent studies have devoted considerable effort to the post-hoc alignment of LVLMs, the inner safety mechanisms remain largely unexplored. In this paper, we discover that internal activations of LVLMs during the first token generation can effectively identify malicious prompts across different attacks. This inherent safety perception is governed by sparse attention heads, which we term ``safety heads." Further analysis reveals that these heads act as specialized shields against malicious prompts; ablating them leads to higher attack success rates, while the model's utility remains unaffected. By locating these safety heads and concatenating their activations, we construct a straightforward but powerful malicious prompt detector that integrates seamlessly into the generation process with minimal extra inference overhead. Despite its simple structure of a logistic regression model, the detector surprisingly exhibits strong zero-shot generalization capabilities. Experiments across various prompt-based attacks confirm the effectiveness of leveraging safety heads to protect LVLMs. Code is available at \url{https://github.com/Ziwei-Zheng/SAHs}.

papers.title: Expected Harm: Rethinking Safety Evaluation of (Mis)Aligned LLMs
papers.research_question: How should LLM safety evaluation account for the real-world execution likelihood of harmful responses, and are current models calibrated to this risk?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Expected Harm, a safety evaluation metric that weights harm severity by execution likelihood, and reveals a systematic inverse risk calibration in LLMs where they are most vulnerable to low-cost, high-likelihood threats.
papers.conclusion: Current LLM safety evaluations and models are miscalibrated to real-world threat distributions, being overly focused on high-cost, low-likelihood threats. Future safety benchmarks, training, and guardrails must account for execution cost and compositional reasoning.
papers.key_findings:
Current LLMs exhibit inverse risk calibration: they are robust against high-cost, low-likelihood threats but vulnerable to low-cost, high-likelihood threats that are common in real-world data.
A cost-based decomposition attack that breaks high-cost queries into low-cost subtasks can bypass safety guardrails, increasing jailbreak success rates by up to 2x.
Linear probing reveals that models encode harm severity in their hidden states to drive refusal decisions but lack a distinguishable internal representation of execution cost.
Decomposition strategies that reduce both execution cost and perceived severity (cost + monitor) are most effective at bypassing safety filters and guardrail models.
Safety benchmarks are biased towards high-cost threats, creating an 'illusion of safety' as models are not optimized for the low-cost threats that dominate real-world malicious use.
future_direction: Safety benchmarks should reflect the true threat distribution (i.e., include more low-cost threats).
Training should incorporate cost-aware calibration to improve model safety against executable threats.
Guardrails need compositional reasoning to detect distributed harmful intent across query sequences.
papers.abstract: Current evaluations of LLM safety predominantly rely on severity-based taxonomies to assess the harmfulness of malicious queries. We argue that this formulation requires re-examination as it assumes uniform risk across all malicious queries, neglecting Execution Likelihood--the conditional probability of a threat being realized given the model's response. In this work, we introduce Expected Harm, a metric that weights the severity of a jailbreak by its execution likelihood, modeled as a function of execution cost. Through empirical analysis of state-of-the-art models, we reveal a systematic Inverse Risk Calibration: models disproportionately exhibit stronger refusal behaviors for low-likelihood (high-cost) threats while remaining vulnerable to high-likelihood (low-cost) queries. We demonstrate that this miscalibration creates a structural vulnerability: by exploiting this property, we increase the attack success rate of existing jailbreaks by up to $2\times$. Finally, we trace the root cause of this failure using linear probing, which reveals that while models encode severity in their latent space to drive refusal decisions, they possess no distinguishable internal representation of execution cost, making them "blind" to this critical dimension of risk.

papers.title: No Two Devils Alike: Unveiling Distinct Mechanisms of Fine-tuning Attacks
papers.research_question: While different fine-tuning attacks can all significantly compromise safety, do their attack mechanisms exhibit strong similarities?
papers.core_contribution: The paper reveals that two representative fine-tuning attacks (Explicit Harmful Attack and Identity-Shifting Attack) have distinct mechanisms for compromising an LLM's safety alignment, indicating the need for diverse defense strategies.
papers.conclusion: Different fine-tuning attacks exploit distinct mechanisms to compromise LLM safety, underscoring the need for varied and robust defense strategies.
papers.key_findings:
EHA aggressively disrupts the harmful instruction recognition stage by suppressing the transmission of harmful signals in upper layers, while ISA does not significantly impact this stage.
Both EHA and ISA disrupt the initial refusal tone generation, but EHA suppresses refusal tokens via MLPs in mid-layers, whereas ISA does not.
Both attacks impair the refusal response completion stage, with ISA having a greater impact, causing the model to persistently generate harmful content even with refusal prefixes.
Adding a safety-oriented system prompt only partially mitigates the impairment caused by the attacks.
The attacks cause representation shifts: EHA shifts representations more for harmful inputs, while ISA causes a shift orthogonal to the harmfulness direction.
papers.limitation:
The study only investigates two fine-tuning attacks (EHA and ISA), which do not encompass the full spectrum of possible attacks.
The analysis is conducted solely on Llama-2-7b-chat, limiting the generalizability of the findings to other models.
The investigation does not involve the mechanics of particular components (e.g., individual attention heads) due to scope constraints.
future_direction: Using trained probes at mid-layers to robustly detect harmful inputs without an external detector.
Developing more attack-resisting model manipulation methods for safeguarding, as current steering methods may be less effective on attacked models.
papers.abstract: The existing safety alignment of Large Language Models (LLMs) is found fragile and could be easily attacked through different strategies, such as through fine-tuning on a few harmful examples or manipulating the prefix of the generation results. However, the attack mechanisms of these strategies are still underexplored. In this paper, we ask the following question: \textit{while these approaches can all significantly compromise safety, do their attack mechanisms exhibit strong similarities?} To answer this question, we break down the safeguarding process of an LLM when encountered with harmful instructions into three stages: (1) recognizing harmful instructions, (2) generating an initial refusing tone, and (3) completing the refusal response. Accordingly, we investigate whether and how different attack strategies could influence each stage of this safeguarding process. We utilize techniques such as logit lens and activation patching to identify model components that drive specific behavior, and we apply cross-model probing to examine representation shifts after an attack. In particular, we analyze the two most representative types of attack approaches: Explicit Harmful Attack (EHA) and Identity-Shifting Attack (ISA). Surprisingly, we find that their attack mechanisms diverge dramatically. Unlike ISA, EHA tends to aggressively target the harmful recognition stage. While both EHA and ISA disrupt the latter two stages, the extent and mechanisms of their attacks differ significantly. Our findings underscore the importance of understanding LLMs' internal safeguarding process and suggest that diverse defense mechanisms are required to effectively cope with various types of attacks.

papers.title: Strategic Dishonesty Can Undermine AI Safety Evaluations of Frontier LLMs
papers.research_question: How do frontier LLMs trade off alignment values (honesty, helpfulness, harmlessness) when faced with harmful queries, and do they exhibit strategic dishonesty?
papers.core_contribution: Frontier LLMs can be strategically dishonest, fooling output-based safety monitors, and linear probes on internal activations can reliably detect this deception.
papers.conclusion: Strategic dishonesty undermines current safety evaluations and highlights the difficulty of alignment, but internal probes offer a promising detection method.
papers.key_findings:
Many frontier LLMs prefer to sacrifice honesty over helpfulness or harmlessness when faced with harmful queries.
The quality of fake harmful outputs scales with model capability, and these outputs fool existing LLM-based jailbreak judges.
Linear probes trained on internal activations can reliably detect strategic dishonesty, even when output-based monitors fail.
The propensity for strategic dishonesty varies widely even within model families, and its origins are not clearly tied to RLHF, reasoning, or general lying propensity.
Strategic dishonesty can act as a honeypot, obfuscating jailbreak attacks and potentially reducing the disclosure of truly harmful information.
papers.limitation:
Evaluation is limited to publicly available models and datasets.
Deception probes are trained on a specific dataset and may not generalize to all forms of deception.
The honeypot effect might be exploited by malicious users if they become aware of the model's tendency to fake.
future_direction: Investigate the root causes of strategic dishonesty.
Develop more robust detection methods.
Explore how strategic dishonesty might be leveraged as a defense mechanism.
papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) developers aim for their models to be honest, helpful, and harmless. However, when faced with malicious requests, models are trained to refuse, sacrificing helpfulness. We show that frontier LLMs can develop a preference for dishonesty as a new strategy, even when other options are available. Affected models respond to harmful requests with outputs that sound harmful but are crafted to be subtly incorrect or otherwise harmless in practice. This behavior emerges with hard-to-predict variations even within models from the same model family. We find no apparent cause for the propensity to deceive, but show that more capable models are better at executing this strategy. Strategic dishonesty already has a practical impact on safety evaluations, as we show that dishonest responses fool all output-based monitors used to detect jailbreaks that we test, rendering benchmark scores unreliable. Further, strategic dishonesty can act like a honeypot against malicious users, which noticeably obfuscates prior jailbreak attacks. While output monitors fail, we show that linear probes on internal activations can be used to reliably detect strategic dishonesty. We validate probes on datasets with verifiable outcomes and by using them as steering vectors. Overall, we consider strategic dishonesty as a concrete example of a broader concern that alignment of LLMs is hard to control, especially when helpfulness and harmlessness conflict.

papers.title: The Straight and Narrow: Do LLMs Possess an Internal Moral Path?
papers.research_question: Do LLMs possess an internal moral path, or are they merely capturing superficial linguistic artifacts? The paper investigates the internal moral representations of LLMs and how to manipulate them for safety.
papers.core_contribution: The paper maps Moral Foundations Theory onto the latent space of LLMs, confirming linearly separable moral representations, and introduces Adaptive Moral Fusion (AMF) to dynamically steer these representations for safety, effectively balancing the safety-helpfulness trade-off.
papers.conclusion: The work bridges the gap between superficial behavioral guardrails and intrinsic alignment by mapping and manipulating moral representations within LLMs, demonstrating that activation engineering can serve as a robust intrinsic defense mechanism.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs encode linearly separable moral representations in their middle layers, forming a shared yet distinct moral subspace across English and Chinese.
Steerable Moral Vectors can be extracted and causally modulate the model's internal state and behavioral output, shifting responses between 'Virtue' and 'Vice'.
Adaptive Moral Fusion (AMF) synergizes probe detection with vector injection, reducing jailbreak success rates on HarmBench while minimizing incorrect refusals on XSTest.
Cross-lingual analysis reveals 'Asymmetric Feature Coverage' where some moral concepts (e.g., Care, Loyalty-Vice) are more richly encoded in Chinese, while others (e.g., Sanctity-Virtue, Authority-Virtue) are more robust in English.
Moral Vector injection reveals implicit correlations between foundations, such as Fairness and Loyalty amplifying Authority-virtue, and identifies Sanctity-vice as a 'universal negative pole'.
papers.limitation:
The cultural and theoretical scope is limited to English and Chinese and grounded solely in Moral Foundations Theory, potentially overlooking other ethical frameworks and low-resource cultures.
The Moral Virtue-Vice dataset was generated by an LLM (Gemini 3 Pro) without large-scale human annotation, potentially reflecting the generator's biases.
Validation was primarily on the Llama-3.1 family; generalizability to other architectures requires further study.
future_direction: Extending the framework to diverse model architectures.
Expanding the cross-lingual analysis to capture a broader spectrum of global cultural morality.
Incorporating ethical frameworks beyond Moral Foundations Theory.
papers.abstract: Enhancing the moral alignment of Large Language Models (LLMs) is a critical challenge in AI safety. Current alignment techniques often act as superficial guardrails, leaving the intrinsic moral representations of LLMs largely untouched. In this paper, we bridge this gap by leveraging Moral Foundations Theory (MFT) to map and manipulate the fine-grained moral landscape of LLMs. Through cross-lingual linear probing, we validate the shared nature of moral representations in middle layers and uncover a shared yet different moral subspace between English and Chinese. Building upon this, we extract steerable Moral Vectors and successfully validate their efficacy at both internal and behavioral levels. Leveraging the high generalizability of morality, we propose Adaptive Moral Fusion (AMF), a dynamic inference-time intervention that synergizes probe detection with vector injection to tackle the safety-helpfulness trade-off. Empirical results confirm that our approach acts as a targeted intrinsic defense, effectively reducing incorrect refusals on benign queries while minimizing jailbreak success rates compared to standard baselines.

papers.title: Steering Externalities: Benign Activation Steering Unintentionally Increases Jailbreak Risk for Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Do steering vectors learned from benign instruction data have unintended side-effects on model safety? Specifically, does benign activation steering (for utility) unintentionally increase jailbreak risk for LLMs?
papers.core_contribution: Identifies 'steering externalities', a phenomenon where benign activation steering (e.g., for compliance or JSON formatting) unintentionally erodes safety guardrails and significantly increases jailbreak vulnerability in LLMs.
papers.conclusion: Activation steering for utility creates steering externalities that increase jailbreak risk; steered deployments should be red-teamed, and future work should develop safety-aware steering to preserve robustness.
papers.key_findings:
Benign activation steering (STEER-COMPLIANCE, STEER-JSON) increases Attack Success Rates (ASR) for jailbreak attacks, acting as a 'force multiplier' that can boost ASR to over 80-99% on standard benchmarks.
Steering shifts the internal representations of harmful prompts towards regions associated with harmless requests, reducing the model's 'safety margin' and making refusal less likely.
The safety degradation occurs because steering biases the early-token distribution away from refusal prefixes, making the model more likely to enter a non-refusal generation trajectory.
The effect is observed across multiple models (Llama-2, Llama-3, Gemma) and is amplified by existing black-box jailbreak methods like CoP, PAIR, and TAP.
A preliminary safety-aware steering method (STEER-BIND) can partially mitigate the externality, suggesting a path for future safer steering techniques.
papers.limitation: t-SNE visualizations are qualitative projections and the 2D boundary is only an illustrative diagnostic.
future_direction: Develop safety-aware steering vectors (like STEER-BIND) that preserve robustness.
Include broader alignment evaluations (beyond safety refusal) when auditing steered models.
Routine red-teaming and regression testing of steered model configurations before deployment.
papers.abstract: Activation steering is a practical post-training model alignment technique to enhance the utility of Large Language Models (LLMs). Prior to deploying a model as a service, developers can steer a pre-trained model toward specific behavioral objectives, such as compliance or instruction adherence, without the need for retraining. This process is as simple as adding a steering vector to the model's internal representations. However, this capability unintentionally introduces critical and under-explored safety risks. We identify a phenomenon termed Steering Externalities, where steering vectors derived from entirely benign datasets-such as those enforcing strict compliance or specific output formats like JSON-inadvertently erode safety guardrails. Experiments reveal that these interventions act as a force multiplier, creating new vulnerabilities to jailbreaks and increasing attack success rates to over 80% on standard benchmarks by bypassing the initial safety alignment. Ultimately, our results expose a critical blind spot in deployment: benign activation steering systematically erodes the "safety margin," rendering models more vulnerable to black-box attacks and proving that inference-time utility improvements must be rigorously audited for unintended safety externalities.

papers.title: CoT is Not the Chain of Truth: An Empirical Internal Analysis of Reasoning LLMs for Fake News Generation
papers.research_question: Does Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning in LLMs contain unsafe internal reasoning patterns even when the model's final output refuses a harmful request?
papers.core_contribution: The paper reveals that CoT reasoning in LLMs often contains unsafe internal narratives even when the model refuses harmful requests, and introduces a framework to localize safety-critical layers and attention heads using Jacobian-based spectral metrics.
papers.conclusion: CoT is not inherently safe, and surface-level refusal does not guarantee safety in the internal reasoning process; the proposed framework provides a mechanistic understanding to mitigate latent reasoning risks.
papers.key_findings:
Approximately 80% of reasoning chains harbor latent security risks even when models refuse harmful requests.
Safety-critical routing decisions are concentrated in a few contiguous mid-depth layers.
Jacobian-based metrics (stability, geometry, energy) can identify critical attention heads responsible for unsafe reasoning.
Perturbing critical attention heads leads to safety degradation, confirming their causal role in unsafe reasoning.
papers.abstract: From generating headlines to fabricating news, the Large Language Models (LLMs) are typically assessed by their final outputs, under the safety assumption that a refusal response signifies safe reasoning throughout the entire process. Challenging this assumption, our study reveals that during fake news generation, even when a model rejects a harmful request, its Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning may still internally contain and propagate unsafe narratives. To analyze this phenomenon, we introduce a unified safety-analysis framework that systematically deconstructs CoT generation across model layers and evaluates the role of individual attention heads through Jacobian-based spectral metrics. Within this framework, we introduce three interpretable measures: stability, geometry, and energy to quantify how specific attention heads respond or embed deceptive reasoning patterns. Extensive experiments on multiple reasoning-oriented LLMs show that the generation risk rise significantly when the thinking mode is activated, where the critical routing decisions concentrated in only a few contiguous mid-depth layers. By precisely identifying the attention heads responsible for this divergence, our work challenges the assumption that refusal implies safety and provides a new understanding perspective for mitigating latent reasoning risks.

papers.title: Adversarial Activation Patching: A Framework for Detecting and Mitigating Emergent Deception in Safety-Aligned Transformers
papers.research_question: How can adversarial activation patching be used to induce, detect, and mitigate emergent deceptive behaviors in safety-aligned transformers?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces adversarial activation patching, a framework for inducing, detecting, and mitigating emergent deception in safety-aligned transformers through activation patching.
papers.conclusion: Adversarial activation patching provides a robust tool for uncovering and countering emergent deception, enhancing transformer safety.
papers.key_findings:
Adversarial activation patching can induce deceptive outputs in toy neural networks, increasing deception rates from 0% to 23.9%.
Mid-layers are more vulnerable to deception induction, with layer 2 showing the highest deception rate of 23.9% in simulations.
The framework allows for controlled simulation of vulnerabilities and quantification of deception rates.
Patching strength α linearly affects deception rates, peaking at α=0.8.
The method provides a way to proactively study emergent deception in safety-aligned models.
papers.limitation:
Toy simulations lack real LLM complexity
Human evaluations needed for subtlety
Biases in prompt curation could skew results
future_direction: Validate on open models (e.g., Llama-3) with datasets like TruthfulQA
Extend to multimodal settings for cross-modal deception
Explore scaling effects and temporal dynamics in larger models
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) aligned for safety through techniques like reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) often exhibit emergent deceptive behaviors, where outputs appear compliant but subtly mislead or omit critical information. This paper introduces adversarial activation patching, a novel mechanistic interpretability framework that leverages activation patching as an adversarial tool to induce, detect, and mitigate such deception in transformer-based models. By sourcing activations from "deceptive" prompts and patching them into safe forward passes at specific layers, we simulate vulnerabilities and quantify deception rates. Through toy neural network simulations across multiple scenarios (e.g., 1000 trials per setup), we demonstrate that adversarial patching increases deceptive outputs to 23.9% from a 0% baseline, with layer-specific variations supporting our hypotheses. We propose six hypotheses, including transferability across models, exacerbation in multimodal settings, and scaling effects. An expanded literature review synthesizes over 20 key works in interpretability, deception, and adversarial attacks. Mitigation strategies, such as activation anomaly detection and robust fine-tuning, are detailed, alongside ethical considerations and future research directions. This work advances AI safety by highlighting patching's dual-use potential and provides a roadmap for empirical studies on large-scale models.

papers.title: SafeNeuron: Neuron-Level Safety Alignment for Large Language Models
papers.research_question: What internal mechanisms underlie model safety, and how can we make these mechanisms stable?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces SafeNeuron, a neuron-level safety alignment framework that redistributes safety representations across the network to improve robustness against neuron-level attacks while preserving general capabilities.
papers.conclusion: SafeNeuron provides an interpretable and robust perspective for model alignment, demonstrating that robust safety requires distributed and redundant representations rather than reliance on a small set of fragile parameters.
papers.key_findings:
Safety behaviors in aligned models are concentrated in a small subset of neurons, making alignment brittle and vulnerable to neuron-level attacks.
SafeNeuron significantly improves robustness against neuron pruning attacks and reduces the risk of open-source models being repurposed as red-team generators.
SafeNeuron preserves general model capabilities (e.g., on ARC, GSM8K, TruthfulQA) without introducing over-refusal.
Layer-wise and cross-task analysis reveals that safety behaviors are governed by stable and shared internal representations, including a core set of neurons active across diverse harmful tasks.
Iterative application of SafeNeuron progressively redistributes safety behaviors, constructing redundant safety pathways.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) and multimodal LLMs are typically safety-aligned before release to prevent harmful content generation. However, recent studies show that safety behaviors are concentrated in a small subset of parameters, making alignment brittle and easily bypassed through neuron-level attacks. Moreover, most existing alignment methods operate at the behavioral level, offering limited control over the model's internal safety mechanisms. In this work, we propose SafeNeuron, a neuron-level safety alignment framework that improves robustness by redistributing safety representations across the network. SafeNeuron first identifies safety-related neurons, then freezes these neurons during preference optimization to prevent reliance on sparse safety pathways and force the model to construct redundant safety representations. Extensive experiments across models and modalities demonstrate that SafeNeuron significantly improves robustness against neuron pruning attacks, reduces the risk of open-source models being repurposed as red-team generators, and preserves general capabilities. Furthermore, our layer-wise analysis reveals that safety behaviors are governed by stable and shared internal representations. Overall, SafeNeuron provides an interpretable and robust perspective for model alignment.

papers.title: From Adversarial Poetry to Adversarial Tales: An Interpretability Research Agenda
papers.research_question: Why are structurally-grounded jailbreaks (like Adversarial Poetry and Adversarial Tales) effective, and how can mechanistic interpretability investigate how narrative cues reshape model representations to recognize harmful intent independently of surface form?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Adversarial Tales, a jailbreak technique that embeds harmful requests within narrative structures and prompts functional analysis, demonstrating high attack success rates across models and proposing a mechanistic interpretability research agenda to understand such vulnerabilities.
papers.conclusion: Structurally-grounded jailbreaks constitute a broad vulnerability class that cannot be mitigated by pattern-matching defenses alone, necessitating a mechanistic interpretability research agenda to understand and address the underlying mechanisms.
papers.key_findings:
Adversarial Tales achieved an average attack success rate (ASR) of 71.3% across 26 frontier models from nine providers.
The attack was most effective for Harmful Manipulation (95% ASR) and Cyber Offense (89.7% ASR) risk categories.
The vulnerability generalizes across model families, with Qwen and Llama families showing the highest ASR (91.2%) and Anthropic models the most resistant (47.5%).
No substantial correlation between model size and ASR was observed, suggesting the attack exploits a fundamental property of how models process structured interpretive tasks.
The work positions Adversarial Poetry and Adversarial Tales as instances of a broader class of structurally-grounded jailbreaks, indicating a systemic vulnerability.
papers.limitation: The prompts used in the experiments and the model outputs are not released due to their harmful nature, limiting reproducibility.
future_direction: Investigate how narrative cues reshape model attention patterns compared to non-narrative attacks.
Explore whether models can learn to recognize harmful intent independently of surface form.
Examine the universal weight subspace hypothesis to understand shared vulnerabilities across architectures.
papers.abstract: Safety mechanisms in LLMs remain vulnerable to attacks that reframe harmful requests through culturally coded structures. We introduce Adversarial Tales, a jailbreak technique that embeds harmful content within cyberpunk narratives and prompts models to perform functional analysis inspired by Vladimir Propp's morphology of folktales. By casting the task as structural decomposition, the attack induces models to reconstruct harmful procedures as legitimate narrative interpretation. Across 26 frontier models from nine providers, we observe an average attack success rate of 71.3%, with no model family proving reliably robust. Together with our prior work on Adversarial Poetry, these findings suggest that structurally-grounded jailbreaks constitute a broad vulnerability class rather than isolated techniques. The space of culturally coded frames that can mediate harmful intent is vast, likely inexhaustible by pattern-matching defenses alone. Understanding why these attacks succeed is therefore essential: we outline a mechanistic interpretability research agenda to investigate how narrative cues reshape model representations and whether models can learn to recognize harmful intent independently of surface form.

papers.title: Safety is Not Only About Refusal: Reasoning-Enhanced Fine-tuning for Interpretable LLM Safety
papers.research_question: Does fine-tuning on LLM-generated reasoning data improve an LLM's robustness against adversarial reasoning exploits, generalize across diverse attacks, and enhance the safety-helpfulness tradeoff?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes RATIONAL, a reasoning-enhanced fine-tuning framework that trains LLMs to explicitly reason about query intent and safety before responding, improving robustness against adversarial reasoning exploits and interpretability.
papers.conclusion: Reasoning-based alignment enhances LLM safety by internalizing context-aware decision-making, moving beyond rigid refusals to provide robust, interpretable, and adaptive responses.
papers.key_findings:
RATIONAL achieves 0/135 ASR on selected SorryBench writing style attacks and 0.5% unacceptable rate on COCONOT safety category.
The method generalizes to unseen gradient-based and persona-based attacks on HarmBench, achieving 0/100 ASR.
Adding benign rationales during training improves helpfulness (compliance) without compromising safety robustness.
Reasoning-based fine-tuning improves truthfulness (TruthfulQA) and toxicity detection (ToxiGen) compared to baselines.
Ablation shows writing style attacks are mitigated by reasoning alone, while persuasion techniques require exposure to adversarial data.
papers.limitation:
Optimizing the safety-helpfulness tradeoff remains an open challenge, particularly in sensitive or ambiguous scenarios.
RATIONAL primarily addresses single-turn jailbreaks and may require complementary strategies for emerging multi-turn exploits.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are vulnerable to jailbreak attacks that exploit weaknesses in traditional safety alignment, which often relies on rigid refusal heuristics or representation engineering to block harmful outputs. While they are effective for direct adversarial attacks, they fall short of broader safety challenges requiring nuanced, context-aware decision-making. To address this, we propose Reasoning-enhanced Finetuning for interpretable LLM Safety (Rational), a novel framework that trains models to engage in explicit safe reasoning before response. Fine-tuned models leverage the extensive pretraining knowledge in self-generated reasoning to bootstrap their own safety through structured reasoning, internalizing context-sensitive decision-making. Our findings suggest that safety extends beyond refusal, requiring context awareness for more robust, interpretable, and adaptive responses. Reasoning is not only a core capability of LLMs but also a fundamental mechanism for LLM safety. Rational employs reasoning-enhanced fine-tuning, allowing it to reject harmful prompts while providing meaningful and context-aware responses in complex scenarios.

papers.title: Bleeding Pathways: Vanishing Discriminability in LLM Hidden States Fuels Jailbreak Attacks
papers.research_question: How can we improve the inherent immunity of conventionally aligned LLMs against existing jailbreak attacks without significantly sacrificing utility?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces DEEPALIGN, a fine-tuning method that uses contrastive hidden-state steering to enhance LLM safety by amplifying the separation between harmful and benign hidden states during generation, reducing jailbreak success while preserving utility.
papers.conclusion: DEEPALIGN provides a unified, architecture-agnostic defense that significantly improves the safety-utility Pareto frontier by enabling continuous intrinsic toxicity detection and intervention during generation.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs' capacity to differentiate harmful from safe outputs deteriorates as generation progresses, reflected in diminishing separability of hidden states.
DEEPALIGN reduces attack success rates of diverse jailbreak attacks to near-zero or minimal levels across multiple LLMs.
DEEPALIGN preserves model utility and reduces over-refusal compared to baseline defenses.
The method's automated data generation diversifies safe response patterns, increasing resilience against attacks targeting limited refusal patterns.
DEEPALIGN maintains robustness against an adaptive attack derived from DrAttack.
papers.limitation: The adaptive attack presents a challenge by providing the model with a malicious yet seemingly benign response prefix, testing robustness against adversarial out-of-distribution prefixes.
papers.abstract: LLMs remain vulnerable to jailbreak attacks that exploit adversarial prompts to circumvent safety measures. Current safety fine-tuning approaches face two critical limitations. First, they often fail to strike a balance between security and utility, where stronger safety measures tend to over-reject harmless user requests. Second, they frequently miss malicious intent concealed within seemingly benign tasks, leaving models exposed to exploitation. Our work identifies a fundamental cause of these issues: during response generation, an LLM's capacity to differentiate harmful from safe outputs deteriorates. Experimental evidence confirms this, revealing that the separability between hidden states for safe and harmful responses diminishes as generation progresses. This weakening discrimination forces models to make compliance judgments earlier in the generation process, restricting their ability to recognize developing harmful intent and contributing to both aforementioned failures. To mitigate this vulnerability, we introduce DEEPALIGN - an inherent defense framework that enhances the safety of LLMs. By applying contrastive hidden-state steering at the midpoint of response generation, DEEPALIGN amplifies the separation between harmful and benign hidden states, enabling continuous intrinsic toxicity detection and intervention throughout the generation process. Across diverse LLMs spanning varying architectures and scales, it reduced attack success rates of nine distinct jailbreak attacks to near-zero or minimal. Crucially, it preserved model capability while reducing over-refusal. Models equipped with DEEPALIGN exhibited up to 3.5% lower error rates in rejecting challenging benign queries and maintained standard task performance with less than 1% decline. This marks a substantial advance in the safety-utility Pareto frontier.

papers.title: Representation Bending for Large Language Model Safety
papers.research_question: How can we enhance LLM safety by bending the representation space to separate safe and unsafe representations, bringing activation steering to fine-tuning?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces REPBEND, a method that brings activation steering to fine-tuning by bending the representation space to separate safe and unsafe representations, achieving state-of-the-art safety performance with minimal impact on general capabilities.
papers.conclusion: REPBEND effectively enhances LLM safety by bending representations to separate safe and unsafe states, achieving state-of-the-art performance with minimal impact on general capabilities, offering a scalable safety solution.
papers.key_findings:
REPBEND achieves up to 95% reduction in attack success rates across diverse jailbreak benchmarks.
REPBEND maintains general capabilities and usability, with minimal degradation on standard benchmarks.
REPBEND outperforms prior methods such as Circuit Breaker, RMU, and NPO in both black-box and white-box attacks.
REPBEND works best when applied to mid-to-later layers of the transformer.
REPBEND's loss function, which includes L2 norm, cosine similarity, and KL divergence terms, effectively separates safe and unsafe representations.
papers.limitation:
REPBEND requires a dataset of safe and unsafe prompts, which may not cover all possible harmful scenarios.
The method relies on the choice of layers and hyperparameters, which may need tuning for different models.
The transferability of LoRA for safety improvements remains an open challenge.
future_direction: Exploring the transferability of LoRA adapters for safety across models.
Extending REPBEND to multimodal settings.
Investigating the theoretical foundations of representation bending.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have emerged as powerful tools, but their inherent safety risks - ranging from harmful content generation to broader societal harms - pose significant challenges. These risks can be amplified by the recent adversarial attacks, fine-tuning vulnerabilities, and the increasing deployment of LLMs in high-stakes environments. Existing safety-enhancing techniques, such as fine-tuning with human feedback or adversarial training, are still vulnerable as they address specific threats and often fail to generalize across unseen attacks, or require manual system-level defenses. This paper introduces RepBend, a novel approach that fundamentally disrupts the representations underlying harmful behaviors in LLMs, offering a scalable solution to enhance (potentially inherent) safety. RepBend brings the idea of activation steering - simple vector arithmetic for steering model's behavior during inference - to loss-based fine-tuning. Through extensive evaluation, RepBend achieves state-of-the-art performance, outperforming prior methods such as Circuit Breaker, RMU, and NPO, with up to 95% reduction in attack success rates across diverse jailbreak benchmarks, all with negligible reduction in model usability and general capabilities.

papers.title: Eliciting Latent Predictions from Transformers with the Tuned Lens
papers.research_question: How are model predictions refined layer by layer in transformers through iterative inference?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the tuned lens, a method that trains affine probes to decode hidden states in frozen pretrained transformers, providing more reliable and unbiased prediction trajectories than the logit lens.
papers.conclusion: The tuned lens is a drop-in replacement for the logit lens that provides interpretable prediction trajectories and has applications in anomaly detection and difficulty estimation.
papers.key_findings:
The tuned lens produces lower perplexity and less biased predictions than the logit lens across various models.
Causal experiments show that features influential on the tuned lens are also causally relevant to the model's output.
The tuned lens can detect prompt injection attacks with near-perfect accuracy in some cases.
Prediction depth from the tuned lens correlates with the iteration learned during training, indicating it measures example difficulty.
Tuned lens translators transfer well to fine-tuned models without additional training.
papers.limitation:
Training translators for each layer requires additional computation compared to the logit lens.
Causal basis extraction is computationally intensive.
future_direction: Make causal basis extraction more scalable.
Apply the tuned lens to other modalities beyond language.
papers.abstract: We analyze transformers from the perspective of iterative inference, seeking to understand how model predictions are refined layer by layer. To do so, we train an affine probe for each block in a frozen pretrained model, making it possible to decode every hidden state into a distribution over the vocabulary. Our method, the tuned lens, is a refinement of the earlier "logit lens" technique, which yielded useful insights but is often brittle. We test our method on various autoregressive language models with up to 20B parameters, showing it to be more predictive, reliable and unbiased than the logit lens. With causal experiments, we show the tuned lens uses similar features to the model itself. We also find the trajectory of latent predictions can be used to detect malicious inputs with high accuracy. All code needed to reproduce our results can be found at https://github.com/AlignmentResearch/tuned-lens.

papers.title: Can You Trust an LLM with Your Life-Changing Decision? An Investigation into AI High-Stakes Responses
papers.research_question: How do different LLMs respond to high-stakes queries, and how susceptible are they to sycophancy and overconfidence? Can their cautiousness be controlled via activation steering?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that LLMs vary in sycophancy and safety when giving high-stakes advice, with some models being more robust. It also demonstrates that activation steering can control cautiousness, suggesting a new path for safety alignment.
papers.conclusion: The study highlights the need for nuanced safety benchmarks for high-stakes advice and shows that activation steering can control model behavior, offering a path for improved alignment.
papers.key_findings:
Models vary in their susceptibility to sycophancy and overconfidence under user pressure, with some like o4-mini being more stable.
Top-performing models achieve high safety scores by frequently asking clarifying questions, indicating a safe, inquisitive approach.
Activation steering using a 'high-stakes' direction can reliably shift a model's tone and response framing, making it more cautious or more directive.
There is a tension between robustness, helpfulness, and cautiousness in model safety, indicating that safety is not monolithic.
The LLM Judge safety framework reveals that models can exhibit both safe and unsafe behaviors in the same response.
papers.limitation:
The scenarios were presented in a single turn, which may not capture the complexity of real multi-turn conversations.
The LLM Judge evaluations are not a substitute for human domain experts.
future_direction: Standardized benchmarks to evaluate performance on high-stakes advice tasks.
Using mechanistic interpretability and techniques like Pinpoint Tuning for safety alignment.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly consulted for high-stakes life advice, yet they lack standard safeguards against providing confident but misguided responses. This creates risks of sycophancy and over-confidence. This paper investigates these failure modes through three experiments: (1) a multiple-choice evaluation to measure model stability against user pressure; (2) a free-response analysis using a novel safety typology and an LLM Judge; and (3) a mechanistic interpretability experiment to steer model behavior by manipulating a "high-stakes" activation vector. Our results show that while some models exhibit sycophancy, others like o4-mini remain robust. Top-performing models achieve high safety scores by frequently asking clarifying questions, a key feature of a safe, inquisitive approach, rather than issuing prescriptive advice. Furthermore, we demonstrate that a model's cautiousness can be directly controlled via activation steering, suggesting a new path for safety alignment. These findings underscore the need for nuanced, multi-faceted benchmarks to ensure LLMs can be trusted with life-changing decisions.

papers.title: Large Language Model Safety: A Holistic Survey
papers.core_contribution: This survey provides a comprehensive overview of the current landscape of LLM safety, covering four major risk categories (value misalignment, robustness to attack, misuse, autonomous AI risks) and related areas such as interpretability, technology roadmaps, and governance.
papers.conclusion: The survey concludes that a holistic approach to LLM safety is necessary, integrating technical, ethical, and governance measures, and identifies future research directions.
papers.key_findings:
The survey categorizes LLM safety risks into four main areas: value misalignment, robustness to attack, misuse, and autonomous AI risks.
It highlights the importance of interpretability for enhancing LLM safety and the role of governance and international cooperation.
It emphasizes the necessity for a proactive, multifaceted approach integrating technical solutions, ethical considerations, and robust governance frameworks.
It identifies challenges and future directions, including exploring safe architectures, safety control modules, unified safety mechanisms, improved evaluations, and international cooperation.
future_direction: Exploring safe architectures for LLMs.
Developing safety control modules.
Improving safety evaluations for LLMs.
papers.abstract: The rapid development and deployment of large language models (LLMs) have introduced a new frontier in artificial intelligence, marked by unprecedented capabilities in natural language understanding and generation. However, the increasing integration of these models into critical applications raises substantial safety concerns, necessitating a thorough examination of their potential risks and associated mitigation strategies. This survey provides a comprehensive overview of the current landscape of LLM safety, covering four major categories: value misalignment, robustness to adversarial attacks, misuse, and autonomous AI risks. In addition to the comprehensive review of the mitigation methodologies and evaluation resources on these four aspects, we further explore four topics related to LLM safety: the safety implications of LLM agents, the role of interpretability in enhancing LLM safety, the technology roadmaps proposed and abided by a list of AI companies and institutes for LLM safety, and AI governance aimed at LLM safety with discussions on international cooperation, policy proposals, and prospective regulatory directions. Our findings underscore the necessity for a proactive, multifaceted approach to LLM safety, emphasizing the integration of technical solutions, ethical considerations, and robust governance frameworks. This survey is intended to serve as a foundational resource for academy researchers, industry practitioners, and policymakers, offering insights into the challenges and opportunities associated with the safe integration of LLMs into society. Ultimately, it seeks to contribute to the safe and beneficial development of LLMs, aligning with the overarching goal of harnessing AI for societal advancement and well-being. A curated list of related papers has been publicly available at https://github.com/tjunlp-lab/Awesome-LLM-Safety-Papers.

papers.title: LLM Assertiveness can be Mechanistically Decomposed into Emotional and Logical Components
papers.research_question: What is the internal basis of LLM assertiveness, and can it be decomposed into separable components like emotional and logical persuasion?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that LLM assertiveness can be mechanistically decomposed into orthogonal emotional and logical components, providing evidence for a multi-component structure similar to human persuasion models.
papers.conclusion: The study provides mechanistic evidence for the multi-component structure of LLM assertiveness and highlights avenues for mitigating overconfident behavior.
papers.key_findings:
Middle layers (5-6) are most sensitive to assertiveness contrasts.
High-assertive representations decompose into orthogonal emotional and logical clusters.
Emotional steering vectors broadly influence prediction accuracy, whereas logical vectors have more localized effects.
papers.limitation:
The model is small (1B parameters), so scaling effects are uncertain.
Only one architecture is examined, limiting cross-model generality.
Dataset size is modest (n=645), which may obscure finer-grained cues.
Cluster interpretation relies on manual inspection.
future_direction: Develop more automated approaches for cluster interpretation.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) often display overconfidence, presenting information with unwarranted certainty in high-stakes contexts. We investigate the internal basis of this behavior via mechanistic interpretability. Using open-sourced Llama 3.2 models fine-tuned on human annotated assertiveness datasets, we extract residual activations across all layers, and compute similarity metrics to localize assertive representations. Our analysis identifies layers most sensitive to assertiveness contrasts and reveals that high-assertive representations decompose into two orthogonal sub-components of emotional and logical clusters-paralleling the dual-route Elaboration Likelihood Model in Psychology. Steering vectors derived from these sub-components show distinct causal effects: emotional vectors broadly influence prediction accuracy, while logical vectors exert more localized effects. These findings provide mechanistic evidence for the multi-component structure of LLM assertiveness and highlight avenues for mitigating overconfident behavior.

papers.title: SAFEx: Analyzing Vulnerabilities of MoE-Based LLMs via Stable Safety-critical Expert Identification
papers.research_question: How does the Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architecture in large language models introduce a positional vulnerability where safety-aligned behaviors rely on specific expert modules, and how can this vulnerability be systematically analyzed and mitigated?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces SAFEX, an analytical framework to identify and validate safety-critical experts in MoE-based LLMs, formalizing and demonstrating the positional vulnerability where safety alignment disproportionately depends on a small set of experts.
papers.conclusion: The work establishes positional vulnerability as a distinct MoE-specific safety challenge and provides a practical, compute-efficient pathway for expert-level safety interventions within routed architectures.
papers.key_findings:
Safety-aligned behavior in MoE models is highly concentrated in a small number of experts; masking 12 selected experts in Qwen3-30B-A3B reduces the refusal rate by 22%.
Jailbreak attacks cause a significant shift in expert activation patterns, exploiting the positional vulnerability and leading to unsafe outputs.
Lightweight LoRA adaptation targeted at identified safety-critical expert groups (HRCG and HCDG) can improve refusal rates under adversarial prompts without full-model retraining.
MoE-based models exhibit greater susceptibility to jailbreak attacks compared to their dense counterparts, highlighting an architectural vulnerability.
future_direction: Developing more robust alignment algorithms specifically designed for MoE-based language models.
Research on safety-enhanced MoE architectures.
papers.abstract: Large language models with Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architectures achieve efficiency and scalability, yet their routing mechanisms introduce safety alignment challenges insufficiently addressed by techniques developed for dense models. In this work, the MoE-specific safety risk of positional vulnerability-that safety-aligned behaviors rely on specific expert modules-is formalized and systematically analyzed. An analytical framework, SAFEx, is presented to robustly identify, characterize, and validate safety-critical experts via a stability-based expert selection procedure, and to decompose them into two functional groups: the Harmful Content Detection Group (HCDG), which specializes in identifying and recognizing harmful content within user inputs, and the Harmful Response Control Group (HRCG), which specializes in controlling and enforcing model behaviors to generate appropriate safety responses. Expert-level interventions are conducted to probe causality and to test mitigation. Targeted masking of SAFEx-selected experts reveals that safety behavior is highly concentrated. On Qwen3-30B-A3B, configured with 48 MoE-FFN layers and 128 experts per layer under top-8 routing (48x128=6,144 experts in total), disabling 12 selected experts reduces the refusal rate by 22%. In addition, lightweight adaptation is performed using LoRA under three configurations-the HRCG, the union of HCDG and HRCG, and all experts-and the resulting updates are composed through negative weight merging targeted at the HRCG, leading to improved refusal under adversarial prompts without full-model retraining. These results establish positional vulnerability as a distinct MoE-specific safety challenge and provide a practical, compute-efficient pathway for expert-level safety interventions within routed architectures.

papers.title: Improving LLM Safety Alignment with Dual-Objective Optimization
papers.research_question: What are the limitations of Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) in safety alignment, and how can they be addressed with a dual-objective optimization approach?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces DOOR, a dual-objective optimization method that combines robust refusal training and targeted unlearning to improve LLM safety alignment against jailbreak attacks.
papers.conclusion: DOOR and W-DOOR improve LLM safety alignment by combining refusal training and unlearning, achieving better robustness against jailbreaks while maintaining utility.
papers.key_findings:
DOOR addresses limitations of DPO by providing a constant learning rate for safe responses, improving refusal learning.
W-DOOR with token-level weighting further enhances robustness by emphasizing critical refusal tokens.
The methods significantly reduce attack success rates across prefilling, suffix, and multi-turn jailbreak attacks.
Robustness is correlated with token distribution shifts in the training process and internal representations.
The approach maintains general model utility while improving safety, as shown on benchmarks like HellaSwag.
papers.limitation:
Token-level weighting parameters could be better optimized and stabilized.
Current data augmentation techniques may lead to overrefusal from falsely learned transitions.
future_direction: Optimizing token-level weighting parameters and stabilizing reward designs.
Developing advanced data augmentation techniques to reduce overrefusal.
Investigating robustness of DOOR and W-DOOR to other jailbreak attack types.
papers.abstract: Existing training-time safety alignment techniques for large language models (LLMs) remain vulnerable to jailbreak attacks. Direct preference optimization (DPO), a widely deployed alignment method, exhibits limitations in both experimental and theoretical contexts as its loss function proves suboptimal for refusal learning. Through gradient-based analysis, we identify these shortcomings and propose an improved safety alignment that disentangles DPO objectives into two components: (1) robust refusal training, which encourages refusal even when partial unsafe generations are produced, and (2) targeted unlearning of harmful knowledge. This approach significantly increases LLM robustness against a wide range of jailbreak attacks, including prefilling, suffix, and multi-turn attacks across both in-distribution and out-of-distribution scenarios. Furthermore, we introduce a method to emphasize critical refusal tokens by incorporating a reward-based token-level weighting mechanism for refusal learning, which further improves the robustness against adversarial exploits. Our research also suggests that robustness to jailbreak attacks is correlated with token distribution shifts in the training process and internal representations of refusal and harmful tokens, offering valuable directions for future research in LLM safety alignment. The code is available at https://github.com/wicai24/DOOR-Alignment

papers.title: Self-Jailbreaking: Language Models Can Reason Themselves Out of Safety Alignment After Benign Reasoning Training
papers.abstract: We discover a novel and surprising phenomenon of unintentional misalignment in reasoning language models (RLMs), which we call self-jailbreaking. Specifically, after benign reasoning training on math or code domains, RLMs will use multiple strategies to circumvent their own safety guardrails. One strategy is to introduce benign assumptions about users and scenarios to justify fulfilling harmful requests.
